name: Desano
confidence_why: Miller (1976, 1999) reports a phonemic Desano 'stress' that coincides with high tone and moves between syllables in minimal pairs, whereas Silva (2012), using vowel-duration measurements and speaker judgments, separates the two and finds stress fixed on the last mora of the root with an independent lexical high tone, an analysis that accounts for Miller's pairs and has not been contested.

catalog_quote: [Miller 1999 sect. 1.12] Stress is also phonemic but is not written in this paper, except where it is needed to distinguish meaning. ... [StressTyp2 carried passage, Miller 1999] The stressed syllable has a high pitch. Stems can have primary, secondary or no stress. In the latter case stress must occur on a suffix, if present. ... [Silva 2012:69] Stress placement in Desano generally follows a straightforward rule: stress falls on the syllable containing the last mora of a noun root morphemes. Since verb roots cannot occur in isolation (i.e., without additional morphology); they do not receive stress. Stress in assigned to verbs only after additional morphology is added to it creating a phonological word. Thus, stress consists of left-to-right exhaustive parsing ... audit.recode_to: From 'conflict' to Silva 2012's predictable pattern (quantity-insensitive iambs parsed L-to-R over moras; primary stress on the root-final (second) mora = head of the leftmost foot; following foot heads secondary; open syllables only, (C)Vʔ/(C)Vh unstressable), with a note that pitch prominence is lexical H/L tone (Miller 1976:110, 1999:15; Silva 2012 sect. 2.3.2.4) — i.e. Miller's 'phonemic stress' = tone placement, not a competing metrical claim. If the catalog prefers to keep 'conflict', at minimum annotate that the disagreement is stress-vs-tone labelling, and read Miller 1999 p.15 before finalizing.

sources.citation: Miller, Marion. 1976. Fonología del desano. In Sistemas fonológicos de idiomas colombianos, Tomo III, 105-111. Lomalinda: Instituto Lingüístico de Verano / Editorial Townsend. (SIL archive entry 19091; via the Internet Archive of sil.org reapdata PDF; no text, scanned at 300 dpi)
sources.quote: p.110: 'El desano tiene dos tonos fonémicos: alto /´/ y bajo, que no se marca. El acento coincide con el tono alto: /séáke/ "cavar", /seáke/ "cortar el cabello", /seaké/ "recoger varas", /ɨ̃́bɨ̃ka/ "humo", /ɨ̃bɨ̃́ka/ "sardinas", /págɨ/ "él golpea", /pagɨ́/ "padre".' Introduction (p.~103): Eastern Tukanoan languages share 'dos niveles fonémicos de tono' and 'cada lengua tiene un sistema propio de ocurrencia de tono y acento.'
sources.locator: p.110 sect. 3.3 'Tono'; also p.106 sect. 2 (syllable = 'unidad de colocación de tono potencial') and p.111 orthography table ('RASGO SUPRASEGMENTAL.. ´ (tono alto).. Se usa únicamente cuando se necesita evitar la ambigüedad')
sources.note: Only dedicated Desano phonology in Glottolog; shows Miller's 'phonemic stress' (1999) is a two-tone H/L analysis in which 'el acento coincide con el tono alto' with lexically contrastive placement (minimal triplets) — makes the Miller-vs-Silva conflict largely a stress-vs-tone terminology difference.
